title: Oasis One: the chair is yours
summary: The parents debate each other and they judge the round alone, fill a ballot and read their RFD out loud, then act one of the Expedition Talk gets its first performance with the Season 1 badge in their hand, and they run the Sprout's rule-maker card.
materials: the sand timers, two minute and one minute, and the call bell
two grown-ups willing to argue against each other for twenty minutes
a blank ballot sheet and a flow sheet ruled into columns
the Season 1 badge, out of its box and in your hand
the Expedition dossier, open at the Talk page
this week's Sprout parent card, and blocks or beads, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: The chair is yours, and nobody is sitting beside you
steps.body:
For three weeks you have been learning what a ballot is, what clash looks like from outside a round, and how to say who won in three sentences. Today the training wheels come off in the least comfortable way: two grown-ups argue, and you are the only judge in the room.

The motion is one you have opinions about. A program that runs is a program that works. You spent this week showing your family a program that ran perfectly and still gave a wrong answer, so you already know which way you lean.

That is the point. Your ballot is not allowed to hold your view. A judge decides the round that happened, not the round they would have run. If the side you disagree with makes the better case and the other side never answers it, you write that down and you sign it. If that stings, that is the job, and you will feel it today.

The shape: constructives two minutes each, rebuttals ninety seconds each, closings one minute each, and no new arguments in a closing. Flow sheet open the whole time, one column per speech. You keep your face still and your pen moving.

When the last bell rings you get four minutes alone with the ballot. Nobody talks to you and nobody asks how it is going. Then you read the decision out loud, to their faces, and you do not soften it and you do not apologise for it.

Hand the device to the two debaters when you reach the next step.

steps.title: For the two debaters only
steps.body:
You two, this step is for you. Hand the device back when you have read it.

You are debating each other today, not them, and they are judging you alone. That reversal is the whole exercise, so it only works if you take it seriously enough to be beaten in front of your child.

The motion: a program that runs is a program that works. Decide sides by coin toss, not by belief, and whoever loses the toss argues the side they like less. Prepare for about ten minutes. Two points each, a reason and an example under each one, and signpost them so a judge can find them on a page.

Three requests. First, clash on purpose: pick up the other side's actual point and answer that one, because a round with no clash gives a judge nothing to weigh and today the judge is young. Second, do not perform for them, and do not lob them a soft ball so they have an easy decision. An easy round teaches them nothing about judging. Third, when the decision comes, take it. No appeal, no but what about, no explaining why they misheard you. You may ask them one question after the ballot is read, and the only question allowed is: what would have changed your mind?

If you find yourself winning too easily, argue harder for your own side rather than easing off, and let the round be lopsided. A judge learning to write why a round was lopsided is learning something real.

steps.title: The ballot and the RFD
steps.body:
Run the round with the timers and the bell, then take your four minutes.

The ballot has three parts and they go in this order, which is not the order it feels like. One: the clash. Name the one place the two cases actually met, in a sentence starting with the words the round came down to. If you cannot find a single place they met, write that down, because that is a real finding about a real round. Two: the weighing. Say who did better in that clash and how you can tell, pointing at something that was said, not at something you believe. Three: the decision. Name the winner in one sentence.

Then read it out loud to both of them. Slowly, whole face up, no shrinking. Then take the one question they are allowed: what would have changed your mind? Answer it honestly, even if the honest answer is that one more example would have done it.

Afterwards, write one private line in your journal that is not on the ballot: did your own opinion about the motion push on the decision, and where did you feel it push? Nobody reads that line but you, and noticing the push is the skill, not being free of it.
checklist: I kept a flow sheet through all six speeches, one column per speech
My ballot names the clash first, then weighs it, then says who won
Every reason in my ballot points at something that was actually said in the round
I read the decision out loud to both of them without softening it
I wrote one private line about where my own opinion pushed on the decision

steps.title: Act one of the Expedition Talk: the forest
steps.body:
The Talk is ten minutes and four acts, one per season, and it gets performed whole in week 12. Today you write and perform act one, so that by the finale you have already stood inside every part of it.

Act one is the forest, which is Season 1, and it runs about under three minutes. Hold the Season 1 badge while you talk. Do not describe it, hold it, and let the room look at it.

Three things to get in, and the order is yours. What you could not do at the start. One thing that went wrong that you can now tell as a story rather than a wound. And the moment the forest ended, whatever you decide that moment was.

One craft note, because you have lived inside this trick for three seasons and now you get to use it. Plant something in act one that you will not pay off until act four. A phrase, an object, a question you leave open on purpose. Do not explain that you are doing it. Write it in the dossier so week 12 remembers what you planted.

Perform it once to whoever is in the room. Then note one line you will cut, because a first draft of a talk is always long and choosing what to leave out is its own skill.
checklist: Act one is written in the dossier, not just in my head
I performed it out loud, holding the Season 1 badge, in about under three minutes
It says what I could not do at the start and how the forest ended
I planted one thing for act four to pay off, and wrote down what it was
I marked one line to cut

steps.title: Teach someone younger
steps.body:
They watched you judge today. Now you hand them a chair of their own.

A parent card is the short card in the app a grown-up normally runs with Sprout. This week it is yours, and this week's card makes them the rule maker: they invent a pattern and the whole family has to copy it while they lead it through the house.

Read the card all the way through before you start, so you know where it lands. Then set it going once yourself, so they see the shape, and then stop leading. Clap, clap, stamp is enough of an example. After that the rule is theirs, whatever they pick, and nobody corrects it.

The part everyone forgets is the middle: partway through, ask them to break their own rule on purpose, once, without warning. Then let them be the one who says caught you. They are young, and being the keeper of a secret is the best part of the game.

Finish with the question that matters, and then wait: what was your rule? Let them say it in their own words, however they say it, and do not tidy it up for them.

Watch for one thing that surprises you: a rule with more parts in it than you expected, or a break so sneaky it fooled a grown-up.
checklist: I read the card all the way through before I started
I showed one example rule and then stopped leading
The rule they paraded was theirs, and nobody corrected it
They broke their own rule on purpose and got to be the one who caught it
I asked what was your rule and waited for them to say it themselves

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt:
Record two things. First, the RFD read out loud to both debaters, whole face in frame, and their one question and your answer to it. Second, act one of the Talk, performed with the badge in your hand.

Then keep rolling for one honest sentence: which of the two cases was harder to judge fairly, and why that one?
